cards.title: ABSTRACT:  Growing concern regarding the impact of fossil fuels has led to demands for the development of green and renewable materials for advanced electrochemical energy storage devices. Biopolymers with unique hierarchical structures and physicochemical properties, serving as an appealing platform for the advancement of sustainable energy, have found widespread application in the gel electrolytes of supercapacitors. In this Review, we outline the structure and characteristics of various biopolymers, discuss the proposed mechanisms and assess the evaluation metrics of gel electrolytes in supercapacitor devices, and further analyze the roles of biopolymer materials in this context. The state-of-the-art electrochemical performance of biopolymer-based hydrogel electrolytes for supercapacitors and their multiple functionalities are summarized, while underscoring the current technical challenges and potential solutions. This Review is intended to offer a thorough overview of recent developments in biopolymer-based hydrogel electrolytes, highlighting research concerning green and sustainable energy storage devices and potential avenues for further development. cards.title: Hierarchically porous materials: synthesis strategies and structure design
cards.authors: Xiaoyu Yang, Lihua Chen, Yu Li, Joanna C. Rooke, Clément Sánchez et al.
cards.summary: Owing to their immense potential in energy conversion and storage, catalysis, photocatalysis, adsorption, separation and life science applications, significant interest has been devoted to the design and synthesis of hierarchically porous materials. The hierarchy of materials on porosity, structural, morphological, and component levels is key for high performance in all kinds of applications. Synthesis and applications of hierarchically structured porous materials have become a rapidly evolving field of current interest. A large series of synthesis methods have been developed. This review addresses recent advances made in studies of this topic. After identifying the advantages and problems of natural hierarchically porous materials, synthetic hierarchically porous materials are presented. The synthesis strategies used to prepare hierarchically porous materials are first introduced and the features of synthesis and the resulting structures are presented using a series of examples. These involve templating methods (surfactant templating, nanocasting, macroporous polymer templating, colloidal crystal templating and bioinspired process, i.e. biotemplating), conventional techniques (supercritical fluids, emulsion, freeze-drying, breath figures, selective leaching, phase separation, zeolitization process, and replication) and basic methods (sol-gel controlling and post-treatment), as well as self-formation phenomenon of porous hierarchy. A series of detailed examples are given to show methods for the synthesis of hierarchically porous structures with various chemical compositions (dual porosities: micro-micropores, micro-mesopores, micro-macropores, meso-mesopores, meso-macropores, multiple porosities: micro-meso-macropores and meso-meso-macropores). cards.title: Layered double hydroxide-based electrocatalysts for the oxygen evolution reaction: identification and tailoring of active sites, and superaerophobic nanoarray electrode assembly
cards.authors: Daojin Zhou, Pengsong Li, Xiao Lin, Adam McKinley, Yun Kuang et al.
cards.summary: The electrocatalytic oxygen evolution reaction (OER) is a critical half-cell reaction for hydrogen production via water electrolysis. However, the practical OER suffers from sluggish kinetics and thus requires efficient electrocatalysts. Transition metal-based layered double hydroxides (LDHs) represent one of the most active classes of OER catalysts. An in-depth understanding of the activity of LDH based electrocatalysts can promote further rational design and active site regulation of high-performance electrocatalysts. In this review, the fundamental understanding of the structural characteristics of LDHs is demonstrated first, then comparisons and in-depth discussions of recent advances in LDHs as highly active OER catalysts in alkaline media are offered, which include both experimental and computational methods. On top of the active site identification and structural characterization of LDHs on an atomic scale, strategies to promote the OER activity are summarised, including doping, intercalation and defect-making. Furthermore, the concept of superaerophobicity, which has a profound impact on the performance of gas evolution electrodes, is explored to enhance LDHs and their derivatives for a large scale OER. In addition, certain operating standards for OER measurements are proposed to avoid inconsistency in evaluating the OER activity of LDHs. Finally, several key challenges in using LDHs as anode materials for large scale water splitting, such as the issue of stability and the adoption of membrane-electrode-assembly based electrolysers, are emphasized to shed light on future research directions.

cards.title: Hydrogen production, storage, utilisation and environmental impacts: a review
cards.authors: Ahmed I. Osman, Neha Mehta, Ahmed M. Elgarahy, Mahmoud Hefny, Amer Al‐Hinai et al.
cards.summary: Abstract Dihydrogen (H 2 ), commonly named ‘hydrogen’, is increasingly recognised as a clean and reliable energy vector for decarbonisation and defossilisation by various sectors. The global hydrogen demand is projected to increase from 70 million tonnes in 2019 to 120 million tonnes by 2024. Hydrogen development should also meet the seventh goal of ‘affordable and clean energy’ of the United Nations. Here we review hydrogen production and life cycle analysis, hydrogen geological storage and hydrogen utilisation. Hydrogen is produced by water electrolysis, steam methane reforming, methane pyrolysis and coal gasification. We compare the environmental impact of hydrogen production routes by life cycle analysis. Hydrogen is used in power systems, transportation, hydrocarbon and ammonia production, and metallugical industries. Overall, combining electrolysis-generated hydrogen with hydrogen storage in underground porous media such as geological reservoirs and salt caverns is well suited for shifting excess off-peak energy to meet dispatchable on-peak demand.

synthesis_notes: Collectively, the pool supports polysaccharide/synthetic-polymer hydrogen-bonded blends, biopolymer–heteropolyacid composites structured by 1‑D clay-like nanofillers, ionic/deep-eutectic plasticising electrolyte families, and inorganic phosphate network solids (glassy proton conductors). Mechanistic coverage is strongest for hydrogen-bond-rich proton-relay environments and confinement/channel-building via nanofillers, plus glassy-network immobilisation concepts. However, direct evidence over the actual cold-to-room window (182–299 K)—including freeze/phase-transition avoidance, bound-fluid mobility near ~200 K, and sub-253 K matrix flexibility—is sparse, and retention/leaching assessments are also under-covered at low temperature. Collectively, the pool supports inorganic hydrogen-bonded network conductors (oxide/phosphate network glasses), polysaccharide-based polymer electrolytes plasticised by eutectic/anti-freeze polar liquids, and water-rich hydrogel electrolyte architectures that suppress ice formation via hydrated confinement. Evidence is strongest at the mechanism/concept level (hydrogen-bond connectivity, freezing suppression) rather than in-operando low-temperature transport datasets. Descriptors that remain under-covered are continuous quantitative transport across ~182–299 K (D1/D2), scaffold glass-transition/low-temperature flexibility metrics (D3), cold-stable acid speciation under confinement (D4), and explicit nanoscale percolation/confinement measurements tied to proton transport (D5) plus leaching/retention quantification (D7). Collectively, the pool supports two main material families: (i) ceramic proton/mixed conductors (perovskite/oxide-type defect chemistries) discussed largely in a high-temperature transport framework, and (ii) polymer electrolyte membranes where a hydrated/acidic conducting phase is structured by soft polymer matrices and nanoscale carbonaceous additives, with some emphasis on hydrogen-bond-rich polysaccharide-like channel formers. Evidence directly aligned to the cold-to-room (182–299 K) window is concentrated in the nanostructured polymer-membrane study reporting subzero conductivity, while the oxide-focused cards mainly inform general trapping/mobility concepts rather than low-temperature continuity. Descriptors that remain under-covered quantitatively across the pool are bound-fluid continuity near ~200 K (D2), matrix mechanical flexibility below ~253 K (D3), and cold-stable acid speciation under confinement (D4), as well as quantified retention/leaching metrics (D7) tied to the cold regime. Collectively, the pool supports polymer–acid composite electrolytes built from hydrogen-bond-rich polysaccharide/amide-type networks, nanoconfining layered silicates and 1‑D tubular clays, and plasticised hydrophilic polymer blends as the main material families. The strongest coverage is on creating dense hydrogen-bond networks, nanoconfinement, and improved acid/water retention (often motivated by fuel-cell stability). Descriptors explicitly tied to the cold window (182–299 K)—especially continuous sub-zero percolation without freezing/segregation (D1), bound-fluid continuity to ~200 K (D2), and matrix flexibility below 253 K (D3)—are under-covered by the provided summaries, with most evidence framed for higher-temperature operation. The pool collectively supports polysaccharide/biopolymer gel and film matrices, clay–polymer nanocomposites (especially fibrous/1‑D clay fillers) and sulfonated polyether-type PEM backbones, with one outlier in inorganic oxide proton conductors at elevated temperature. Evidence is mostly about conductivity enhancement and proposed transport mechanisms rather than cold-window thermophysical stability. Descriptors that remain under-covered are the cold-to-room phase-continuity requirement (no freezing/segregation), bound-fluid mobility down to ~200 K, sub‑253 K matrix flexibility/glass-transition behavior, and cold-stable acid speciation/retention with quantified leaching/volatility. Collectively, the pool spans hydrophilic polymer blends (synthetic water-soluble polymers plus polysaccharides), acid- or salt-doped polymer electrolytes with inorganic oxide nanoparticle fillers (nanocomposite free-volume/confinement concepts), and a separate family of inorganic/ceramic proton conductors; it also includes a broad review pointer to 2D layered carbides/nitrides as potential confinement scaffolds. However, the pool is thin on direct evidence in the 182–299 K window for suppression of freezing/segregation, persistence of a mobile bound-water/plasticiser fraction, and low-temperature mechanical (sub‑253 K) flexibility. It also under-covers cold-stable acid speciation within confinement and quantitative retention/leaching data for the conducting phase. Collectively, the pool mainly supports broad design concepts around hierarchically porous architectures, polymer nanocomposites with high-aspect-ratio nanofillers (including layered clays and carbonaceous nanofillers), and layered inorganic hydroxide families, but it does not directly evidence low-temperature proton-conducting electrolyte behavior. As a result, critical cold-window descriptors tied to preserved percolation and non-freezing conducting phases (D1–D4) and their supporting nanoconfinement/retention mechanisms (D5–D7) are under-covered by direct, quantitative electrolyte measurements. The literature here is therefore more useful as generic structural/processing background for building confined, percolated networks than as component-level proof of cold-stable proton transport. Across this pool, the only broadly relevant material families are (i) self-assembled colloidal/periodic porous architectures discussed in the context of photonic crystals and (ii) ionic-liquid/ion-conducting electrolyte materials discussed for alkali-ion batteries, plus general electrochemical materials coverage for supercapacitors. None of the cards, as summarized here, provide direct evidence for cold-to-room proton-transport continuity, bound-water/antifreeze retention, flexible polymeric scaffolds, confined acid speciation, or nanoconfined hydrated-acid percolation. As a result, descriptors D1–D7 are collectively under-covered by the provided summaries, especially the low-temperature (182–299 K) proton-conduction and confinement requirements.
